what_its_for: Benazepril is used to treat high blood pressure (hypertension). Lowering your blood pressure helps prevent strokes, heart attacks, and kidney problems. It belongs to a group of medicines called ACE inhibitors, which help relax your blood vessels so your heart does not have to work as hard.
how_to_take: Take benazepril by mouth with or without food, usually once or twice a day. Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water. Try to take it at the same time every day so it becomes part of your routine. Do not skip doses even if you feel fine, because high blood pressure often has no symptoms.
dosing: Your doctor will start you on a low dose and may slowly increase it based on how well your blood pressure is controlled. The usual starting dose for adults is 10 mg once a day. The typical maintenance dose ranges from 20 mg to 40 mg per day, either as one dose or split into two doses. Never change your dose on your own without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do NOT take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one, as this can cause your blood pressure to drop too low.
storage: Store benazepril at room temperature, between 59°F and 77°F (15°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused medicines down the toilet — ask your pharmacist about proper disposal.
what_to_avoid: Avoid using salt substitutes or potassium supplements unless your doctor tells you it is okay, because benazepril can raise potassium levels in your blood. Avoid drinking alcohol, as it can increase the blood-pressure-lowering effect and make you feel dizzy or faint. Be careful when standing up quickly from a sitting or lying position, especially when you first start taking this medicine. Avoid non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) like ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin) or naproxen (Aleve) without asking your doctor, as they can reduce the effectiveness of benazepril and harm your kidneys. Do not take benazepril if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant — it can seriously harm an unborn baby.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat (this is called angioedema and is a rare but serious reaction); difficulty breathing or swallowing; a sudden drop in blood pressure causing dizziness or fainting; signs of high potassium such as muscle weakness or irregular heartbeat; decreased urination or swelling in your legs or feet suggesting kidney problems; a dry, persistent cough that bothers you (this is a common side effect — your doctor may switch you to a different medicine); or if you think you might be pregnant.
when_it_works: Benazepril begins to lower your blood pressure within 1 to 2 hours after your first dose. You may notice its full effect within 2 to 4 weeks of regular use. Even if you feel well, keep taking your medicine every day. High blood pressure is a long-term condition, and stopping suddenly can cause your blood pressure to rise quickly.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Do NOT use benazepril during pregnancy. It can cause serious injury or death to an unborn baby. Tell your doctor immediately if you become pregnant. Breastfeeding: Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding, as small amounts of the drug may pass into breast milk. Elderly patients: Older adults may be more sensitive to the blood-pressure-lowering effects and may need a lower starting dose. Kidney disease: Your doctor may need to adjust your dose if you have kidney problems. Children: Benazepril can be used in children 6 years and older for high blood pressure, but the dose will be determined by your child's doctor based on weight.
